entries.text: credit-2026-11-02 credit Friday Bond & Credit Deep Dive · post-week review 2026-11-02 Research verified 2 Nov · week ended 30 Oct; not Friday 08:00 knowledge Verified extract The new post-week review verifies Microsoft final pricing, adds P&G issuance terms and examines BIS cross-border credit and Bank of England non-bank research. Prior Friday editions remain archived. Friday Bond & Credit Deep Dive · post-week review Week ended 30 October 2026 · research verified 2 November This newly completed scheduled edition includes final issuance documents and the completed week. It is not a reconstruction of information available at 08:00 Singapore time on Friday. This public extract retains only independently checked material; the earlier 30 October edition is unchanged. 1. Microsoft: final pricing replaces preliminary borrowing context Microsoft's SEC pricing sheet is dated 29 October, with expected settlement on 4 November. Eight fixed-rate tranches total US$23bn; two floating-rate tranches of US$1bn each bring the offering to US$25bn. The following are issue terms, not current market quotes. Maturity · USD principal · coupon · issue price per 100 · issuance YTM · stated benchmark spread 2036 · $4bn · 5.550% · 99.659 · 5.595% · +65bp 2046 · $2bn · 6.150% · 99.624 · 6.183% · +85bp 2056 · $4bn · 6.250% · 99.919 · 6.256% · +95bp 2066 · $2bn · 6.350% · 99.914 · 6.356% · +105bp The 2066 note is benchmarked to the Treasury due May 2056, not a 40-year Treasury. The floating-rate notes use compounded SOFR plus a margin; no fixed YTM is inferred for them. 2. Non-AI corporate issuance P&G's 26 October SEC document specifies four USD tranches totalling US$4bn. Its 2056 tranche has a 5.900% coupon, 99.860 issue price, 5.910% issue YTM and +60bp over its stated Treasury benchmark. Four verified P&G tranches are added to the existing 26–27 October monitor; Microsoft is detailed separately above because it priced on 29 October. 3. Cross-border credit is a dated stock, not delinquency BIS statistics released 29 October place cross-border bank credit at US$40.7tn at end-June 2026, with 11% annual growth. The Q2 increase was US$877bn: US$560bn in loans/deposits and US$317bn in bank-held debt securities. These global banking aggregates are not U.S. household arrears or current November credit losses. 4. Non-bank transmission and AI financing The Bank of England's 23 October Working Paper 1212 models banks and non-bank intermediaries using UK data. Conventional rate-policy transmission changes little with non-bank size in the model, while QE transmission depends on how that sector expands. This is model-based research, not an observed default forecast. The BIS AI-financing bulletin connects long-term borrowing, off-balance-sheet structures and institutional funding. Its event-study findings do not establish a persistent Treasury-yield increase caused by AI issuance. 5. Analysis and coverage limits Separate duration risk, issuer credit risk and funding risk. Review legal borrower, collateral priority, liquidity and cash interest coverage. A downgrade, late payment, nonaccrual and realised investor loss are different events. Existing household-credit metrics retain their Q2 2026 label. New rating-action ratios, private-credit default estimates and unverified financing terms were omitted from this extract; no personal account amounts or borrowing balances are included. These are individual surveys with different methods and samples. Their margins are not probabilities and differences across pollsters are not daily changes. 4. Legal developments Reuters reported on 30 October that the Justice Department sought to prevent certification after a narrow Republican loss in Alaska, based on disputed allegations about a similarly named candidate. State officials challenged the lawsuit, and Peltola's campaign had denied involvement. These are allegations and legal proceedings, not findings of election fraud. The briefing highlights certification uncertainty as a risk to the timing of a clear Senate outcome. 5. Completed U.S. equity session At the 30 October U.S. close, the S&P 500 ended at 7,580.07, down 1.82%, and the Nasdaq Composite at 25,437.00, down 2.86%. Intel fell 28.6%. These values were checked against Reuters' closing-market report carried by AOL, updated 20:23 UTC. Reuters linked the sell-off to disappointing Intel and Amazon results and concerns about AI spending. These are session-close observations, not Saturday live quotes. 6. FX reference snapshot The ECB's 30 October EUR reference rates were USD 1.1172, SGD 1.4282 and CHF 0.9194 per EUR. Dividing each non-USD rate by the USD rate gives USD/SGD 1.2784 and USD/CHF 0.8230, rounded to four decimals. These are calculated reference crosses, not New York closing prices or executable bank rates. 7. Conditional market implications The briefing separates election scenarios from an automatic directional trade. A Democratic sweep may increase fiscal confrontation; divided control may constrain legislation while leaving budget negotiations unresolved; Republican control leaves fiscal, inflation and issuance risks to assess. These are conditional interpretations, not observed returns or forecasts of bond prices. Monitor duration, funding currency and collateral together. Falling Treasury yields may support existing bonds, while CHF appreciation can increase the USD value of CHF liabilities. A favourable move in one variable does not remove the other risks. No client positions, borrowing amounts or allocations are included. 8. Publication checks and limits The 30 October election source-unavailable record remains in edition history. entries.text: earnings-2026-10-30 earnings US Earnings Reuters Daily 2026-10-30 08:29 SGT cutoff Cloud and AI growth remained strong, while cash burn and weak guidance drove sharp reactions. US Earnings Command Centre Friday, 30 October 2026 08:29 SGT cutoff Reported: 28–29 Oct US | Upcoming: 30–31 Oct US | NYSE/Nasdaq only MARKET'S BIGGEST STORY AI growth is accelerating. Investors are punishing the cash burn. Amazon delivered its fastest AWS growth in nearly five years. Intel beat quarterly earnings expectations. Yet both sold off sharply after hours as investors focused on spending, cash generation and weak forward guidance. reuters.com +1 INTC • After-hours −23% Guidance / cash burn AMZN • After-hours −7% Intraday AH low LLY • Regular +6%+ Strong drug sales Reuters-reported moves on 29 October, at the time of each article. Amazon fell as much as 7%; Intel fell 23% after hours; Eli Lilly climbed more than 6% during trading. These are not live quotes. reuters.com +2 1. Earnings tone | Last two days Polarised, with exceptionally demanding expectations The clearest theme is the divergence between strong underlying sales and weaker forward profitability or cash flow. Intel, Amazon and Caterpillar illustrate disappointment despite areas of solid operating demand. Eli Lilly, Mastercard and Cheniere benefited from stronger end-market conditions. reuters.com +3 Resilient demand: AWS +39%, Linde electronics sales +15%, Mastercard cross-border volume +11%, and strong obesity-drug demand at Eli Lilly. reuters.com +3 Pressure points: AI infrastructure capital expenditure, Intel production constraints, PC demand weakness, transport costs and margin sustainability. reuters.com +2 A Reuters-verified, market-wide beat/miss percentage for only 28–29 October was not established. The companies discussed are selected for significance, not a complete earnings-season sample. 2. Top earnings movers | Mega caps and major reactions Intel (INTC) −23% AH Q3 results • 29 Oct • Semiconductors Adjusted EPS $0.52 / $0.40 est. Revenue $16.51bn $16.50bn est. Guidance miss: Q4 sales $15bn–$16bn versus $17.07bn expected; Q4 adjusted EPS $0.25 versus $0.43 expected. Why it fell: manufacturing shortages, weak PC demand, factory disruption and expected cash burn. Reuters, 29 Oct. reuters.com Amazon (AMZN) As much as −7% AH Q3 results • 29 Oct • Cloud and consumer AWS revenue $46bn +39% YoY Trailing 12m FCF −$42.4bn Guidance: Q4 revenue $240.0bn–$247.0bn, against $244.51bn consensus. The midpoint is below consensus, although the range includes it. Capex: $77.26bn for the third quarter, with 2026 planned spending of $220bn and materially more expected in 2027. Why it fell: heavy investment overwhelmed operating cash generation despite AWS acceleration. Full-company EPS comparison not established from the Reuters article reviewed. reuters.com Eli Lilly (LLY) More than +6% Q3 results • 29 Oct • Healthcare Adjusted EPS $7.48 Revenue $24.4bn Guidance: 2026 revenue raised to $91bn–$92bn; adjusted EPS outlook reduced to $35–$36 because of acquisition-related charges. Why it rose: strong Mounjaro and Zepbound sales and higher annual revenue expectations. Reuters confirmed earnings and revenue beats but the retrieved report did not establish exact consensus figures for both. reuters.com Other significant earnings reactions Stock Reaction Reuters-linked driver Alphabet (GOOGL) −12% Ad weakness / AI cash burn Caterpillar (CAT) −8% Cost and outlook concerns Mastercard (MA) +4%+ Payment volume resilience Cheniere (LNG) +5% LNG exports / raised outlook Alphabet's Thursday regular-session move followed its 28 October results. Caterpillar's 8% drop was reported during Thursday trading. Reuters figures at publication, not synchronized closing prices. reuters.com +3 3. AI / Semis / Tech | Earnings and outlook AI cash generation: the widening gap Quarterly free cash flow, US$ billion $-15bn $-5bn $5bn $15bn $25bn Microsoft Alphabet Microsoft: Free cash flow $18.6bn Alphabet: Free cash flow $-9.1bn Both quarters ended September 2026. Amazon's trailing-12-month −$42.4bn is excluded because the period differs. Reuters +2 Microsoft +$18.6bn vs $8.54bn est. Alphabet −$9.07bn Second negative quarter Microsoft (MSFT) | Strongest cash-flow signal Azure grew 48% to $33.17bn versus $32.84bn expected. Adjusted EPS was $4.89 versus $4.73 expected; revenue was $92.28bn. Its next-quarter Azure growth forecast of 49%–50% exceeded the 47.6% consensus. Quarterly capex was $45.2bn, below the $50bn plan because of delayed infrastructure deliveries, not a confirmed reduction in the buildout. Reuters Alphabet (GOOGL) | Cloud growth, advertising miss Google Cloud revenue more than doubled to $30.71bn. Consolidated revenue of $127.6bn missed $128.2bn expected; adjusted EPS was $2.67 against $3.02 expected. Advertising revenue was $82.01bn, around $1.4bn short of expectations. Google Cloud backlog reached $561bn, but Alphabet anticipates significantly higher 2027 capex and near-term margin pressure. Reuters Cybersecurity and software | Disruption concerns Reuters reported Fortinet (FTNT) falling 26% after slower product revenue growth and a reduced annual services forecast. ServiceNow (NOW) declined 23% after a quarterly profit miss outweighed improved subscription revenue and cash-flow margin guidance. Analysts also questioned the pace of AI-related revenue contributions. reuters.com Strategy interpretation AI infrastructure demand is not disappearing. The market is distinguishing between suppliers, platforms generating cash, and businesses funding expansion through continued investment or borrowing. The important second-order question is whether today's backlog converts into profitable cash receipts before financing costs rise further. 4. Consumer & industrials | Real-economy read Caterpillar (CAT) −8% Reported during US trading $7.20 EPS vs $7.08 expected Record backlog: $78.1bn Linde (LIN) $4.59 Adjusted EPS vs $4.52 est. $9.4bn sales Up 9% Electronics sales: +15% Caterpillar: Maintained its 2026 revenue-growth forecast in the mid- to high-teens, despite exceptionally strong power-generator demand from data centres. Reuters identified tariffs, diesel prices and slower manufacturing-capacity expansion as constraints. Its record backlog rose $6bn sequentially. reuters.com Linde: Raised its 2026 adjusted EPS forecast to $17.82–$17.92 from $17.70–$17.90. Semiconductor manufacturers' demand for high-purity gases supported growth, although the new guidance assumes a 2% currency benefit. reuters.com Amazon consumer read: Advertising grew just 12% to $19.6bn versus expected growth of 18%. Management cited the shift in Prime Day timing, while Reuters connected its holiday-quarter guidance to pressure from higher household costs and fuel prices. reuters.com Interpretation: Industrial orders can remain healthy while profits suffer from rising production costs. Consumer spending can remain positive while margins and advertising growth disappoint. 5. Financials | Payments and private credit Mastercard (MA) More than +4% Adjusted EPS $5.31 vs $5.16 est. Cross-border volume +11% Quarterly growth Spending remained resilient across income groups. Reuters reported that higher gasoline prices supported nominal spending growth, although continued inflation could eventually constrain discretionary purchases. reuters.com Blue Owl Capital (OWL) Distributable EPS $0.24 vs $0.23 Total AUM $330bn Record New capital $12.6bn Q3 commitments Blue Owl's direct-lending originations reached $5.2bn. Reuters linked investor concerns about private-credit companies to AI disruption, technology borrowers and potential defaults, even as Blue Owl reported record fundraising. reuters.com Bank credit-risk distinction: These earnings establish payments resilience and private-credit fundraising strength, but do not establish a market-wide improvement in delinquencies, default rates or bank loan provisions. No such extrapolation is made. 6. Healthcare / Energy / Other sectors Merck (MRK) | Pipeline and oncology Adjusted EPS $2.49 vs $2.08 expected; revenue $18.1bn vs $17.3bn expected. Keytruda sales reached $8.6bn; Winrevair rose 94% to $694m. Merck raised 2026 adjusted EPS guidance to $2.77–$2.82 and its revenue floor to $66.8bn. Risk: Keytruda patent expiry beginning in 2028, requiring successful diversification. reuters.com Bristol Myers Squibb (BMY) | Mixed guidance Adjusted EPS $1.35 vs $1.14 expected; revenue $13.1bn vs $12.75bn expected. Raised its annual revenue forecast to $49.75bn–$50.25bn but cut adjusted EPS guidance to $6.35–$6.55 because of acquisition-related charges. Risk: Pipeline progress and the return from acquisition spending. reuters.com Cheniere Energy (LNG) | Energy supply disruption Third-quarter LNG revenue rose 41.8% to $6.1bn, and exports increased 15.3% to 188 cargoes. Raised adjusted 2026 core-profit guidance to $8.75bn–$9.25bn. Reuters reported shares up 5% as disrupted Middle Eastern gas supplies increased demand for US LNG. Risk: Geopolitical and LNG pricing sensitivity; strong current margins may not be permanent. reuters.com 7. Guidance & expectations watchlist Reported outlook changes and expectations from Reuters, US$ unless stated otherwise. Company 2026 / forward guidance Signal Microsoft Azure Q2 growth 49%–50% vs 47.6% est. Above est. Intel Q4 revenue $15bn–$16bn vs $17.07bn est. Below est. Amazon Q4 sales $240bn–$247bn vs $244.51bn est. Midpoint below Eli Lilly Annual sales $91bn–$92bn Raised Eli Lilly Annual EPS $35–$36 Reduced Merck Annual EPS $2.77–$2.82 Raised Bristol Myers Annual EPS $6.35–$6.55 Reduced Linde Annual EPS $17.82–$17.92 Raised Cheniere Adjusted core profit $8.75bn–$9.25bn Raised Reuters earnings reports, 28–29 October. Amazon's range includes consensus even though its midpoint is below it. Eli Lilly's and Bristol Myers' EPS reductions reflect acquisition-related charges, not necessarily deterioration in underlying demand. Reuters +7 Next 48 hours | Earnings to watch ExxonMobil (XOM) Friday, 30 October • US Upcoming Reuters' pre-earnings signals Possible refining uplift +$4.5bn Versus prior quarter Possible upstream drag −$1.3bn Versus prior quarter Reuters' 16 October preview, based on Exxon's filing, linked stronger refining economics to supply disruptions but also identified weaker upstream commodity pricing. Full results are scheduled for 30 October. These are pre-result indications, not actual earnings. reuters.com The retrieved Reuters reporting did not sufficiently establish precise upcoming consensus estimates for other 30–31 October companies. Those figures are deliberately omitted rather than imported from non-Reuters earnings calendars. No additional Saturday earnings event is confirmed in the selected Reuters coverage. 8. Earnings → macro | Rates, credit and financing AI financing is moving into bond markets Microsoft bond deal ~$25bn Reported planned issuance Orders received $100bn+ As reported by Reuters Reuters reported on 29 October that Microsoft was preparing its first US investment-grade bond sale in more than nine years, potentially across maturities of two to 40 years. The offering size was not final. The borrowing illustrates how even highly cash-generative AI companies are increasingly considering external capital to finance infrastructure while preserving flexibility. reuters.com Rates / duration: Larger long-maturity corporate issuance creates more duration supply. Its effect on Treasury yields or credit spreads cannot be inferred from the deal size alone. Credit quality: Microsoft's strong cash flow contrasts with Amazon's trailing cash burn and Intel's near-term cash-flow warning. Debt capacity should be assessed through operating cash generation, capex obligations and refinancing costs. Inflation and supply costs: Reuters linked elevated energy prices to pressure on household expenditure and transportation margins, while higher refining and LNG margins supported energy producers. reuters.com +2 Singapore portfolio translation: For a USD bond portfolio financed in CHF or SGD, separate three risks: underlying issuer credit quality, long-duration price sensitivity and funding-currency exposure. Strong AI revenue does not automatically protect all three. 9. Top three client talking points | Next 48 hours 01 Theme: Cash flow matters more than headline AI growth Microsoft generated $18.6bn in quarterly free cash flow. Amazon and Alphabet experienced substantial cash burn despite accelerating cloud demand. Action: Review cash-flow sustainability alongside revenue growth and AI backlog. 02 Risk: Positive earnings surprises may still be sold Intel exceeded Q3 EPS expectations but forecast a disappointing fourth quarter. Fortinet and ServiceNow suffered sharp stock moves as investors questioned future performance. Action: Evaluate forward guidance, margin quality and balance-sheet capacity before reacting to an EPS beat. 03 Opportunity and risk: AI financing versus energy cash generation Technology issuers are increasing capital requirements while certain energy producers benefit from tighter physical supply and stronger pricing. Action: Compare free cash flow after capex, leverage and debt costs across sectors rather than treating all earnings growth as equally valuable. Reuters links used Primary news articles and Reuters pre-earnings coverage. Exxon's 16 October article is included solely for its still-relevant 30 October preview. entries.title: Friday Bond & Credit Deep Dive
entries.text: credit-2026-10-30 credit Friday Bond & Credit Deep Dive 2026-10-30 08:09 SGT delivery Duration, AI borrowing, new issuance and the path from late payment to default. Friday Bond, Credit & Debt Markets ────•❉᯽❉•──── 30 October 2026 · 8:00 AM SGT Weekly research Research cutoff: 29 October 2026, U.S. market close, subject to source publication availability. Primary focus: 23–29 October. Earlier studies are explicitly labelled as background. Executive market dashboard 10Y U.S. Treasury 4.98% 29 Oct · −2bp vs 23 Oct 30Y U.S. Treasury 5.32% 29 Oct · −1bp vs 23 Oct U.S. IG credit OAS 86bp 5bp tighter vs 23 Oct U.S. HY credit OAS 314bp 24bp tighter vs 23 Oct Treasury par yields as of 29 Oct; ICE BofA credit-index spreads as of 28 Oct, the latest published observations verified. Sources: U.S. Treasury and FRED. U.S. Department of the Treasury +2 The central development this week is the growing scale and complexity of AI debt financing, not a broad collapse in credit markets. Microsoft moved toward a reported US$25 billion bond transaction, banks and Blackstone arranged US$63 billion of AI-equipment financing for Anthropic-related infrastructure, and new BIS research documented how AI borrowing can affect insurers, private-credit funds and potentially Treasury term premiums. Meanwhile, the broad high-yield index spread actually tightened during the week. Investment interpretation: Credit stress is becoming more issuer-specific and structure-specific, while the public market remains receptive to stronger borrowers. That divergence matters. A credit index can improve while an individual leveraged AI borrower suffers a severe financing shock. 1. U.S. Treasury duration and credit spreads Latest verified yield curve Maturity 23 Oct 29 Oct Change 2Y 4.68% 4.61% −7bp 5Y 4.84% 4.78% −6bp 7Y 4.91% 4.87% −4bp 10Y 5.00% 4.98% −2bp 20Y 5.36% 5.35% −1bp 30Y 5.33% 5.32% −1bp Official U.S. Treasury par yield curve. U.S. Department of the Treasury The curve remains relatively steep from 2Y to 30Y, but the far end offers little additional yield over the 20Y point. On 29 October, the 30Y yielded 3bp less than the 20Y. For a long-duration investor, the extra ten years of maturity must therefore be justified by the bond's valuation, convexity and expected yield path, not by assuming that longer maturity necessarily pays more. Credit spreads: the index is not confirming systemic panic U.S. high-yield credit spreads ICE BofA U.S. High Yield Index OAS, basis points. Latest available observation: 28 October 2026. 310bp 320bp 330bp 340bp 350bp 22 Oct 23 Oct 26 Oct 27 Oct 28 Oct 22 Oct: HY option-adjusted spread 340bp 23 Oct: HY option-adjusted spread 338bp 26 Oct: HY option-adjusted spread 330bp 27 Oct: HY option-adjusted spread 318bp 28 Oct: HY option-adjusted spread 314bp Source: FRED high-yield OAS. St. Louis Fed Index 23 Oct 28 Oct Weekly move IG corporate OAS 91bp 86bp −5bp HY corporate OAS 338bp 314bp −24bp HY less IG OAS 247bp 228bp −19bp The difference between the indexes is a simple comparison, not a duration-adjusted relative-value measure. Positioning implication: Broad HY spread tightening suggests risk appetite remained resilient through the week. That is not an invitation to buy every issuer offering a double-digit yield. The more important question is whether default probabilities, collateral coverage and refinancing prospects are diverging faster than index averages reveal. 2. Institutional research deep dive Four substantive studies and data releases were selected, including two from 23–29 October and two earlier October papers retained for their importance. A fifth Fitch credit review is included with its publication-date limitation. Research 1. BIS: Building AI on Credit Building AI on credit: structures and spillovers BIS Bulletin No. 140 · 27 October 2026 · 8-page full PDF Mathias Drehmann and Egemen Eren This is the week's most directly relevant central-bank research. BIS finding Figure Projected 2026 capex by five major U.S. hyperscalers Over US$800bn Gross bond issuance by those five firms through September US$222bn AI-linked off-balance-sheet bonds/ABS reportedly placed during 2026 US$75–100bn Estimated data-centre lease commitments, mid-2026 US$1.2tn Portion related to leases not yet commenced US$820bn These figures represent different financing categories and should not be added together as though they were all outstanding bonds. bis.org How AI borrowing risk can travel through the financial system AI hyperscalers and technology customers Lease commitments · capacity contracts · limited guarantees Data-centre and equipment SPVs Buildings · power infrastructure · GPUs · contracted revenue Banks Senior loans and construction finance Non-bank investors Private credit · insurers · ABS Simplified structure based on BIS Graph 2, not a representation of any one transaction. The BIS analysed 18 AI-financing news days during 2026. It found an estimated 1.5bp increase in the 10-year Treasury term premium on those days, generally fading within two trading days. This is an event-study association, not a demonstrated causal or persistent effect. The paper's Graph 3 and online annex explain the methodology and limitations. bis.org Why it matters: Long-dated AI corporate debt competes for some of the same institutional capital that buys Treasuries and other long-duration bonds. The immediate measured effect is small. Persistent issuance on this scale could still influence how much compensation investors demand for holding duration. Client talking point: AI investment is now large enough to matter to bond markets, even for investors who own no AI shares. Research 2. S&P: North American data-centre debt dashboard S&P Global Ratings launches interactive North America data center dashboard 23 October 2026 · Official research release and rated-transaction dataset S&P's newly published dashboard covers its rated North American data-centre transactions. 32 Rated transactions $105.3bn Total debt issuance 8.7 GW Tenant capacity Debt issuance across S&P's rated universe Corporate finance Project finance Structured-finance ABS Project finance: 58.3% Structured-finance ABS: 26.4% Corporate finance: 15.3% S&P reports 143 supporting properties and warns that power access, permitting and development constraints may affect project delivery. These figures cover S&P-rated transactions, not the entire data-centre financing market. Oct 23, 2026 Implication: The largest part of the measured debt is project finance, where the exact lender claim, sponsor support and project cash flow deserve scrutiny. The important due-diligence distinction is between a bond issued directly by a profitable hyperscaler and a security issued by a separate data-centre company that happens to have that hyperscaler as a tenant. Research 3. BIS: Bank regulation and private-credit growth Bank liquidity regulation and the growth of private credit BIS Working Paper No. 1388 · October 2026, released 20 October · 48-page PDF · Prior-week research Authors: Sebastian Doerr, Gaston Gelos and Vesa Pursiainen. The researchers examined how U.S. bank liquidity regulation changed the provision of credit. Their central finding: A one-standard-deviation higher historical exposure to banks affected by liquidity requirements was associated with nearly 50% greater private-credit lending volume after the regulatory changes, relative to the comparison counties. bis.org This is a historical empirical estimate, not a claim that private credit grew by 50% in 2026. Credit implication: Lending risk did not simply disappear when banks became subject to tougher liquidity requirements. Some financing shifted toward non-bank vehicles. For portfolio analysis, that means reviewing the entire credit intermediation chain, especially when banks also provide leverage to the funds that ultimately hold the loans. Client talking point: Better-regulated banks do not necessarily mean every form of borrowing has become safer. Risk can migrate to institutions with different funding and transparency requirements. Research 4. Fitch: Business development company credit quality Fitch Ratings Completes Peer Review of 8 US BDCs Fitch original page dated 15 October · Research findings redistributed 28 October · Full Fitch access restricted The accessible Fitch-distributed summary states that seven BDC issuer ratings were affirmed, while New Mountain Finance's outlook moved from Stable to Negative. Indicator Finding Average realised loss rate, Fitch-rated BDCs, full-year 2025 1.1% Same group, first half 2026 0.5% First-half 2026 loss rate for the reviewed peer group 0.4% The periods are not the same length. The 0.5% first-half figure should not be compared mechanically with the 1.1% full-year figure as proof that losses have halved. Fitch expects continuing asset-quality pressure and identifies nonaccrual loans as a risk. The Lead Implication: Public BDC filings may reveal stress earlier than headline aggregate private-credit default statistics, but realised losses, nonaccruals, fair-value marks and interest coverage must be considered together. Research 5. Bank of England: Who buys long-duration corporate bonds? Domestic and foreign insurer corporate bond demand and monetary policy Staff Working Paper No. 1,210 · 9 October 2026 · 59-page PDF · Background research The study uses security-level insurer transactions from 2018–2022. It finds that UK and U.S. life insurers can respond very differently to changes in bond yields. For example, in the researchers' historical estimates, a 1 percentage-point rise in the UK 10-year government-bond yield was associated with higher net buying by UK insurers but reduced demand from U.S. insurers for their relevant UK-corporate-bond holdings over subsequent months. bankofengland.co.uk Implication: Long-duration debt demand is segmented by currency, regulatory treatment and liabilities. A 30-year bond may not have the same natural buyer base as a five-year bond. Methodological limit: Historical UK/US insurer evidence is not a forecast of October 2026 U.S. Treasury yields. 3. Latest Reuters debt and borrowing developments Microsoft: reported US$25bn bond offering Reuters · 29 October 2026 Reuters reported a planned sale of approximately US$25bn, with more than US$100bn in orders and up to ten tranches spanning roughly 2–40 years. Its SEC preliminary prospectus confirms the offering structure but leaves final pricing terms blank. Reuters +1 Classification: Announced/marketed offering. Exact coupon and final issuance yield not verified from the reviewed primary filing. Anthropic/Broadcom: US$63bn structured equipment financing Reuters · 26 October, updated 27 October 2026 Banks and Blackstone announced financing for an SPV to purchase AI chips and network equipment. Reuters reported around US$43.5bn first-lien senior debt, with second-lien capital involving Blackstone and residual-value support from Broadcom. Reuters Classification: Financing arrangement, not an ordinary unsecured corporate bond. Coupon, all-in yield and individual loan maturities were not disclosed. Oracle: attempts to cap future funding requirements Reuters · 28 October 2026 Oracle said it expects to need up to US$20bn of additional financing for the remainder of fiscal 2027, split between debt and equity. It reported US$125.34bn in notes payable and other borrowings as of 31 August. Its goal is positive free cash flow in the second half of fiscal 2028. Reuters Classification: Funding plan and management forecast, not a newly issued US$20bn bond. Two additional transactions deserve attention: Reuters reported that SpaceX secured US$40bn of chip-related debt financing with an Apollo affiliate on 26 October, while Argentum AI was only in talks for a proposed US$5bn chip financing deal on 27 October. These must not be counted as equally completed borrowing events. Reuters Moody's also told Reuters on 27 October that 17% of 607 borrowers in its tracked sample used payment-in-kind interest, while the 2027–2029 refinancing period remained a concern for weaker borrowers. Reuters 4. New issuance and borrowing monitor The table below uses actual final pricing term sheets wherever available. These are issue-date terms, not live secondary-market yields. All amounts USD. Issue price is per 100 of face value. UST benchmark yield and issue spread are quoted together. N/V = not verified in the reviewed source. Issuer / pricing date Amount · Maturity Coupon Issue price Issue YTM UST benchmark yield / spread United Rentals · 26 Oct $700m · 15 Oct 2029 5.550% 99.922 5.580% 4.780% / +80bp United Rentals · 26 Oct $800m · 15 Oct 2031 5.750% 99.884 5.778% 4.828% / +95bp United Rentals · 26 Oct $1bn · 15 Oct 2036 6.200% 99.710 6.240% 4.990% / +125bp Texas Instruments · 26 Oct $500m · 9 Nov 2028 5.000% 99.827 5.092% 4.712% / +38bp Texas Instruments · 26 Oct $500m · 9 Nov 2031 5.350% 99.779 5.401% 4.821% / +58bp CBRE Services · 27 Oct $500m · 15 Jan 2032 5.650% 99.424 5.782% 4.832% / +95bp CBRE Services · 27 Oct $500m · 15 Jan 2037 5.900% 97.872 6.186% 4.986% / +120bp Main Street Capital · 27 Oct $500m · 15 Jan 2030 6.550% 99.258 6.800% 4.800% / +200bp KeyCorp · 27 Oct $1bn · 2 Nov 2032 5.889% initially 100.000 5.889% initial fixed pricing 4.839% / +105bp Sources: Original SEC/issuer pricing documents. sec.gov +4 Special point on KeyCorp: Its coupon becomes floating for the final year, at compounded SOFR +130bp. The quoted 5.889% fixed-rate pricing figure is not a guaranteed fixed YTM across the entire note's life. Ratings and financing purposes Issuer Credit ratings verified Borrowing structure / purpose United Rentals Moody's Baa3 / S&P BBB− Senior unsecured; specific proceeds not verified in pricing sheet Texas Instruments N/V in reviewed term sheet Senior notes linked to an acquisition, with special mandatory redemption provisions CBRE Services Moody's Baa1 / S&P BBB+ / Fitch BBB+ Senior unsecured; general corporate purposes, including commercial-paper repayment and acquisition-related uses Main Street Capital S&P BBB− / Fitch BBB− BDC unsecured notes; initially repay revolving-credit borrowing KeyCorp N/V in reviewed term sheet Fixed-to-floating senior bank debt Microsoft N/V in preliminary prospectus Proposed senior unsecured debt; general corporate purposes including capital requirements Anthropic-related SPV N/V Senior and second-lien AI-equipment financing SpaceX-related financing N/V Chip-related debt, as reported by Reuters SEC +4 What the pricing tells us The verified spread dispersion is substantial: Spread on newly priced USD debt Spread above each deal's stated Treasury benchmark. Issue-date spreads, not live OAS. 0bp 55bp 110bp 165bp 220bp Texas Instruments 2… Texas Instruments 2… United Rentals 2029 CBRE 2032 KeyCorp 2032 CBRE 2037 United Rentals 2036 Main Street Capital… Texas Instruments 2028: Issue spread 38bp Texas Instruments 2031: Issue spread 58bp United Rentals 2029: Issue spread 80bp CBRE 2032: Issue spread 95bp KeyCorp 2032: Issue spread 105bp CBRE 2037: Issue spread 120bp United Rentals 2036: Issue spread 125bp Main Street Capital 2030: Issue spread 200bp Selected issuance spreads sourced from final pricing term sheets above. Different maturities, issuer risk, capital structures and investor liquidity make this a descriptive comparison rather than a pure credit-risk ranking. Main Street Capital's +200bp spread is particularly noteworthy beside the relatively small issuance concessions for Texas Instruments. But the higher spread is not simply free income. A BDC owns portfolios of loans to businesses and its own funding conditions reflect both asset quality and financing risk. For context, Main Street says proceeds will initially refinance existing revolving facilities. That illustrates an important distinction between gross debt issuance and net additional borrowing. 5. Loan delinquencies, defaults and late-payment watch Latest verified national household dataset New York Fed Q2 2026, published 11 August 2026. Infrastructure leasing, tenant quality and long-term debt repayment risks. Final investment assessment Three observations stand out. First, Treasury duration and corporate credit should not be conflated. A 30-year government bond can lose substantial market value without any credit deterioration, while an IG corporate issuer may face additional spread widening. Second, AI debt is increasingly being transformed through project vehicles, equipment collateral and financial guarantees. The borrower, asset owner, customer and ultimate risk-bearer may be different entities. The BIS and S&P research make that distinction particularly important. Third, the credit cycle should be monitored through cash payments, not only ratings and quoted yields. Rising PIK utilisation, weakening loan cures, higher nonaccruals and refinancing dependence can reveal deterioration before headline defaults rise. For bond positioning: Preserve liquidity and collateral headroom, accumulate long duration selectively, favour transparent credit structures, and require meaningful compensation for subordinated or illiquid exposures. For client conversations: A higher coupon is not the same as a safer investment. The relevant question is whether the borrower can continue paying and whether the investor can hold the security through volatility without being forced to sell. entries.title: Three questions before any market headline
entries.text: starting-point Three questions before any market headline Start here Ask what is happening in the economy, what is already priced into investments, and what reaches your own pocket. These reports become easier to understand once the three questions are kept separate. The economy describes activity, jobs and prices. Markets put a price today on an uncertain future. Your personal outcome also depends on the price you paid, the currency you spend, fees, financing and when you need your money back. Strong growth can coexist with a disappointing investment return if buyers already paid for even better growth. A highly rated borrower can issue a bond whose market price swings sharply. An overseas portfolio can gain in its own currency yet deliver a much smaller gain in SGD. These are different mechanisms, so a single green or red headline is usually inadequate. Use the MAS October review to understand Singapore’s current growth, inflation and policy backdrop. Use JPMorgan to explain global markets and investment mechanics. Use MAS, GIC and Temasek annual reports to understand institutional roles and measurement. The three supplied written reports are secondary analyses: their claims need the underlying official sources. The reading order in this briefing follows those links. It moves from growth and inflation to equities, rates and credit, then currency, public finances, institutions and private markets. All quoted numbers retain the source’s own displayed precision. A source-published rounded figure is not converted into a falsely exact economic measurement. A useful market update explains a cause, a possible consequence and a decision to monitor. It should help the reader ask a better question. The review date of this briefing is 31 October 2026. The charts are dated snapshots, not live prices or a claim that all figures describe the same day. Begin each client discussion with spending currency, time horizon, cash needs and ability to withstand a temporary loss. mas-macro jpm-markets jpm-alternatives Explanation with dated evidence

entries.title: Why strong Singapore growth can still feel uneven
entries.text: singapore-growth Why strong Singapore growth can still feel uneven Singapore Technology is doing much of the heavy lifting; a strong national figure does not mean every sector is thriving. The MAS October review reports Q3 2026 GDP growth of 5.4% year on year and 1.1% quarter on quarter after seasonal adjustment. These are advance estimates. The two figures answer different questions: the first compares with the same quarter a year earlier; the second compares with the immediately preceding quarter after removing recurring seasonal patterns. Technology-related industries accounted for around 75% of year-on-year growth in Q3, according to MAS. That is a share of the increase in output, not a claim that technology is 75% of Singapore’s economy. The same page identifies technology-related industries as 22.1% of nominal value added in 2025. Confusing the level of activity with its contribution to growth would substantially overstate the sector’s size. The practical picture is an uneven expansion. Electronics, machinery, related trade and information services benefit from AI investment. Other parts of the economy face different demand and cost conditions. MAS describes weakness in some consumer-facing businesses and pressure on oil-related industries even while the headline economy expands. MAS expects the technology expansion to continue into 2027 at a more measured pace. This is its baseline assessment, not a promise. A slowdown in growth means output is rising less quickly; it does not automatically mean a recession. The vulnerability is that a narrower engine leaves the economy more exposed if AI spending or its financing disappoints. Think of a company whose best division generates most of the additional profit. The company can be growing strongly while other divisions struggle. Do not treat strong GDP as a buy signal for every Singapore company, property or fund. Sector earnings, balance sheets and prices still differ. Watch whether growth broadens beyond technology, whether semiconductor orders hold up, and whether jobs and household spending follow. mas-macro mas-oct2026-p21 Published observations and MAS outlook

entries.title: Why MAS cares about the SGD basket
entries.text: inflation-sgd Why MAS cares about the SGD basket Singapore Singapore uses the exchange rate to help control imported inflation; USD/SGD is only one part of that policy picture. MAS Core Inflation rose from 1.5% in Q2 2026 to 2.1% in July–August. The October review forecasts core inflation of 1.5–2.0% for 2026 and 1.5–2.5% for 2027. These are forecasts for annual averages, not a ceiling on every monthly reading. Core inflation excludes accommodation and private transport; it is not identical to a particular household’s cost-of-living change. Inflation describes how fast prices rise. If inflation slows, prices can still be increasing. It is the difference between climbing stairs more slowly and going back downstairs. Energy, food, transport, wages, subsidies and competition can move differently, so the components matter as much as the headline. MAS maintained the prevailing appreciation rate of the S$NEER policy band in October 2026, after tightening in April and July. S$NEER is a trade-weighted currency measure. The bilateral USD/SGD rate is the price of one currency against another. An appreciating basket can coexist with SGD weakness against a particular currency, because the other basket currencies also move. For households, a stronger SGD can soften imported costs. For an investor with unhedged overseas assets, it can reduce the value translated back into SGD. Those effects can occur together. MAS’s policy objective concerns price stability in Singapore; maximising the SGD accounting return on foreign reserves is a different objective. The review’s inflation research separates external demand, external supply and domestic forces. It estimates that external factors explain about 68% of the inflation variation captured by its model over the sample. That is a model-based historical decomposition, not a statement that 68% of each household bill is imported. The policy implications depend on the source and persistence of the shock. The same stronger dollar that makes some imported goods cheaper can make an overseas investment look smaller on an SGD statement. A fall in USD/SGD alone does not measure the full MAS policy stance. Neither the basket path nor the inflation forecast guarantees a particular future FX rate. Separate a household’s SGD cash requirements from long-term foreign assets. Read the latest policy decision alongside inflation components and actual bilateral rates. mas-macro mas-oct2026-p10 mas-oct2026-p29 Published data and labelled forecasts

entries.title: Who pays for the AI buildout
entries.text: ai-financing Who pays for the AI buildout Equities Demand can be strong while the bill for future capacity rises even faster than cash generation. JPMorgan’s page 22 groups Alphabet, Amazon, Meta, Microsoft and Oracle. It shows total company capital expenditure of US$416 billion in 2025, with consensus forecasts of US$799 billion in 2026, US$1,093 billion in 2027 and US$1,200 billion in 2028. The last three are forecasts. The measure is total company capex, not a directly measured AI-only spending total. Operating cash flow is cash generated from running a business. Capital expenditure pays for long-lived assets such as equipment and buildings. On the slide, free cash flow is operating cash flow minus capex. A company can report accounting profit while free cash flow is weak because it is spending heavily on future capacity. That does not by itself prove insolvency, but it changes the funding question. MAS provides a useful second view. Page 23 compares semiconductor production conditions with a composite indicator of hyperscalers’ capacity to sustain capex. The latter considers cash-flow margins, leverage and investment intensity. Its company universe differs from JPMorgan’s and includes CoreWeave. These are analytical indices, not an observable default probability or a reproducible bank credit score. The connection is straightforward: suppliers can enjoy strong orders today while customers take on larger financing commitments. If future AI revenue justifies the spending, the expansion may endure. If monetisation disappoints, buyers may reduce capex, lenders may demand better terms and suppliers may face weaker orders. MAS describes this as a downside risk, while judging near-term backlogs and commitments supportive. For a portfolio, inspect the shared economic exposure. Technology equities, semiconductor suppliers, data-centre property, power infrastructure and private credit to the same ecosystem may all respond to one investment cycle. Different product labels do not ensure different underlying risks. A restaurant can be busy and profitable while borrowing heavily to open many new outlets. The question is whether the new outlets eventually earn enough to justify the cost. Large capex is neither proof of a bubble nor proof of an attractive investment. Aggregate cash-flow charts cannot establish whether an individual borrower can service its debts. Track cash generation against capex, debt and lease commitments, refinancing needs, customer contracts and actual monetisation. Keep each issuer’s analysis separate. jpm-markets mas-macro jpm-gtm-p22 mas-oct2026-p23 Historical observations, forecasts and risk analysis

entries.title: Does owning hundreds of shares spread risk evenly
entries.text: equity-concentration Does owning hundreds of shares spread risk evenly Equities An index can own many names while a small group still drives much of its value. At 30 September 2026, JPMorgan shows the ten largest S&P 500 constituents at 40.6% of market capitalisation and 36.1% of trailing earnings. A market-cap-weighted index puts more money into larger companies. Counting the number of holdings therefore does not tell you how evenly the risk is spread. The earnings share also matters. The largest companies contribute substantial profits as well as substantial market value. Concentration alone does not prove prices are irrational. It tells you which companies and business drivers can most influence results, and where earnings disappointment could be consequential. JPMorgan’s valuation page reports a forward P/E of 19.0 times against its 30-year average of 17.2 times. Forward P/E is price divided by forecast earnings. A higher ratio means paying more for each unit of expected profit. If the earnings forecast changes, the valuation can change even without a move in the share price. CAPE, also shown in the guide, uses a long historical average of inflation-adjusted earnings. It is a different measurement, so its number should not be compared directly with forward P/E as if one were an alternative price quote. Valuation measures help frame expectations; they do not provide a date for a market correction. For a Singapore investor, add a currency lens. A U.S. index chart generally describes the U.S. market in USD. The return in SGD depends on the exchange rate and any hedging. Owning an S&P 500 fund, a technology fund and several megacap shares may add overlapping exposure rather than meaningful new diversification. A supermarket basket with hundreds of items can still be dominated by a few expensive purchases. The number of items does not determine where most of the money went. A historical average is not a fair-value guarantee. Concentration can persist, and expensive markets can keep rising. Review the largest underlying holdings across all funds and direct shares. Compare business drivers, regions, currencies and valuation assumptions before adding another product. jpm-markets jpm-gtm-p8 jpm-gtm-p5 30 September 2026 snapshot

entries.title: Why a strong borrower can have a volatile bond
entries.text: bond-duration Why a strong borrower can have a volatile bond Bonds Credit quality concerns repayment; duration concerns how much the price moves when required yields change. A fixed-rate bond promises a stream of payments. If comparable new bonds offer a higher yield, buyers usually pay less for the old payment stream. If required yields fall, the old stream becomes more attractive. The issuer can remain financially sound throughout this repricing. Maturity is the date principal is due. Duration measures sensitivity to a change in yield. A long maturity and low coupon often leave more of a bond’s value dependent on distant payments, increasing its rate sensitivity. Convexity describes the bend in the price–yield relationship; it explains why a simple straight-line estimate becomes less accurate for larger moves. JPMorgan page 34 illustrates total-return scenarios under a parallel shift in the yield curve. The printed figures below show how the range widens at longer maturities. The slide does not explicitly state the scenario horizon, so these should be described as the publisher’s illustrations, not independently verified one-year forecasts. Long yields are influenced by more than the next central-bank meeting. Inflation expectations, the compensation for holding long debt, government borrowing needs and supply can all matter. MAS’s October financial-conditions chapter describes rising long government yields even alongside resilient equity markets. Holding to maturity changes the decision if contractual payments are met and the investor can hold. It does not remove inflation, currency, funding or collateral risk. A financed investor might be forced to sell before maturity, turning an interim price fall into a realised loss. This is why duration must be assessed together with liquidity and borrowing terms. A reliable tenant does not make the resale price of a long rental contract stable when market rents and interest rates change. These publisher illustrations are not prices or P&L forecasts for a specific Temasek or Treasury holding. They exclude the investor’s own FX, fees, financing and margin arrangements. Compare duration and maturity separately. entries.title: Is a high bond yield good compensation for risk
entries.text: credit-spread Is a high bond yield good compensation for risk Bonds A bond can offer a high total yield while paying only a small extra amount for the company’s credit risk. A useful breakdown is a government or near-risk-free reference yield plus compensation for credit, liquidity and other bond features. This is a pricing guide, not an exact universal identity. Credit spread is not the coupon and not the entire yield. One basis point equals 0.01 percentage point. JPMorgan page 36 shows investment-grade option-adjusted spreads of 80 basis points versus a 144 basis-point long-run average in its chart. High-yield spreads are 311 basis points versus 498. Yet displayed yields to worst are 6.0% and 8.3%. Much of the attractive-looking yield therefore comes from the wider interest-rate environment, while the extra credit compensation is relatively narrow. This distinction matters when deciding between taking more duration and taking weaker credit. They expose the portfolio to different problems. Government yields can rise even if an issuer’s business is healthy. Credit spreads can widen even if government yields are unchanged. Both can happen together. An average spread does not establish the value of an individual bond. Seniority, covenants, cash flows, refinancing dates, liquidity and recovery prospects differ. The default chart on the same JPMorgan slide also uses different treatment of distressed exchanges across some categories. A reader should retain that methodology rather than turning the chart into a simple ranking of all default risks. The base rental market can be expensive even when the extra rent for accepting a troublesome tenant is small. Total income and compensation for a particular risk are different questions. Tight spreads do not prove an imminent sell-off. High yield does not guarantee a sufficient cushion against defaults or spread widening. Compare the extra yield with the specific risk being accepted. For each issuer, examine cash coverage, maturity schedule, debt structure and the liquidity available to exit. jpm-markets jpm-gtm-p36 30 September 2026 snapshot Investment grade High yield Option-adjusted spread 80 bps 311 bps Long-run average in chart 144 bps 498 bps Displayed yield to worst 6.0% 8.3% Figures retain the source’s displayed precision. entries.title: Why a USD gain can shrink in SGD
entries.text: fx-return Why a USD gain can shrink in SGD Currency The investment return and the currency conversion multiply; they do not simply subtract. Define the exchange rate as SGD received for one USD. If an investment’s USD value changes by r and this exchange rate changes by f over the same measurement period, a simplified return with no intermediate external flows is (1 + r) × (1 + f) − 1 in SGD. This convention matters: quoting the inverse exchange rate changes the calculation. The supplied USD sensitivity report uses a 5.60% USD return and a 3.00% annual USD decline against SGD over a matched annualised horizon. The exact arithmetic is 1.056 × 0.97 − 1 = 0.02432 = 2.432%. The original report displayed 2.43% because it explicitly rounded to two decimal places. This briefing preserves the exact computed value. There is a major interpretation limit. GIC’s 5.6% is a historical twenty-year annualised USD return, not a next-year forecast. Pairing it with assumed future FX weakness is a conditional illustration. It does not reveal GIC’s direct net USD position, currency hedges or an expected future SGD return. Changing the reporting currency of a diversified global portfolio is also different from measuring how much the portfolio is economically exposed to one currency. Non-USD assets can themselves rise in USD terms when USD weakens. Company revenues, costs, borrowing and hedging can pull in different directions. For an actual bond portfolio, coupon payment dates, conversion rates, fees and financing cash flows require their own dated ledger. A simple terminal-return identity should not be used to silently approximate those flows. For a household, the relevant question remains what purchasing power is available in the currency of future spending. The investment can grow in dollars while each dollar buys fewer Singapore dollars. Both steps affect the final SGD result. The 3% FX move is a stated scenario from the supplied analysis, not a forecast by MAS. The institutional reports do not disclose enough to estimate a precise common USD sensitivity for MAS, GIC and Temasek. Show investment P&L, income, FX effects, fees and financing separately, then reconcile them. Match the currency and horizon before comparing returns. gic-2026 mas-2026 temasek-2026 Assumed annual USD weakening USD return assumption Exact converted SGD return 0% 5.60% 5.6% 1% 5.60% 4.544% 2% 5.60% 3.488% 3% 5.60% 2.432% 4% 5.60% 1.376% 5% 5.60% 0.32% Derived from inputs already shown in supplied Report 2. Assumes matched annualised horizons; not a forecast, institutional exposure estimate or bond/loan simulation. Explicit conditional arithmetic

entries.title: Where Singapore’s government revenue comes from
entries.text: public-finances Where Singapore’s government revenue comes from Singapore Taxes and other operating revenue are one stream; the permitted investment-return contribution is another. A household analogy helps: recurring earnings fund spending, while accumulated savings can also generate income. Singapore’s system has a specific constitutional framework, so the analogy should not be taken as an exact household budget. The important distinction is between the reserve principal, investment returns and the amount available for annual spending. The audited FY2025/26 government accounts show operating revenue of S$130,049,822,095.34 and Net Investment Returns Contribution of S$27,522,875,864.50. Adding those two reported values gives S$157,572,697,959.84. This sum describes revenue before deducting expenditure; it is not the fiscal surplus or a measure of total reserves. IRAS collections are already inside government operating revenue. IRAS’s 4 September 2026 release reports S$97.3 billion collected in FY2025/26, up 9.4%, representing 74.8% of government operating revenue at the release’s published precision. Adding that S$97.3 billion again would count much of the same revenue twice. NIRC includes up to 50% of expected long-term real returns on relevant net assets invested by GIC, MAS and Temasek, plus up to 50% of net investment income on remaining past reserves. Real means after inflation. Relevant net assets account for government liabilities. It is not simply half of this year’s combined accounting profit or dividends. This approach helps smooth spending across market cycles. A weak investment year does not mechanically cut the budget by the same amount. Persistent changes in asset values or expected long-term returns can still affect resources over time, so smoothing does not mean markets are irrelevant. Land-sale proceeds add to reserves rather than ordinary spendable operating revenue. The supplied revenue report was prepared in August 2026. Its statement that the latest IRAS series ends at FY2024/25 is now outdated. Its FY2026/27 total of approximately S$163.23 billion is derived using rounded components; MOF’s own published total is S$163.24 billion. Use the publisher’s aggregate at its stated precision and retain the rounding caveat. Keep FY2026/27 budget estimates separate from FY2025/26 audited actuals. The spending allowance from a long-term investment pool is not the same as the pool’s market gain in one year. Do not add IRAS to operating revenue, treat land-sale receipts as ordinary tax revenue, or add MAS, GIC and Temasek totals into a national-wealth figure. Internal claims and different measurement bases would need reconciliation. Use AGD for audited actuals, MOF for the current budget and NIRC rules, and IRAS for agency collections. Preserve fiscal-year labels and classification changes. budget-actual budget-estimate iras-2026 nirc reserves FY2025/26 audited values SGD Operating revenue 130,049,822,095.34 NIRC 27,522,875,864.50 Sum of the two revenue components 157,572,697,959.84 AGD Statement of Budget Outturn, physical PDF page 17 / printed page 9. Sum is calculated exactly from the displayed audited amounts; it is not the budget surplus. Audited actuals with separately labelled estimates

entries.title: How MAS can have an FX drag and still make a profit
entries.text: mas-accounts How MAS can have an FX drag and still make a profit Currency Currency translation is one part of the result; investment gains, liquidity-management costs and other expenses also matter. MAS holds foreign reserves for central-bank purposes while reporting its accounts in SGD. A foreign-currency asset can be unchanged in its own units yet translate into fewer SGD when SGD strengthens. That alone does not remove the foreign currency available for policy operations. The supplied FY2024/25 infographic is an accessible example: investment gains of S$31.4 billion, negative currency translation of S$3.4 billion and net money-market-operation and other costs of S$8.3 billion produce reported net profit of S$19.7 billion at the infographic’s displayed precision. It is a historical year, not the October 2026 result. The separately verified FY2025/26 MAS speech reports investment gains of S$39.8 billion, translation drag of S$16.4 billion, net money-market-operation and other costs of S$2.4 billion and a S$1.0 billion Consolidated Fund contribution. The reported net profit is S$20.0 billion. Showing only the S$16.4 billion drag would give an incomplete picture. The FY2021/22 statements provide the opposite historical example: an overall loss despite positive investment gains. That year’s main translation effects involved EUR, JPY and GBP. FY2025/26’s explanation principally involves USD and JPY. It would be inaccurate to describe all three years as simply USD losses. There are further measurement distinctions. MAS’s accounts have Group and Authority columns; its accounting investment result is not a fully comparable fund NAV total return. Liquidity operations incur interest costs and have policy objectives. A Consolidated Fund contribution, a later distribution of profit and NIRC are different fiscal concepts. For an individual who needs SGD to pay a mortgage or school fees, an FX translation reduction can be economically important. The fact that MAS can continue to conduct policy with its foreign assets does not imply a household should ignore its own currency mismatch. Read the whole income statement. A large deduction can coexist with a positive final result when other gains are larger. Headline amounts use issuer rounding. The FY2021/22 cost definition differs from later net-cost figures, so do not force those rounded components into a common exact waterfall. Net USD exposures and full hedges are not disclosed. Pair FX effects with the total result, state the affected currencies and period, and distinguish institutional policy capacity from personal SGD purchasing power. mas-2025-info mas-2025-accounts mas-2022-accounts mas-2022-info mas-2022-speech mas-2026 mas-fy2025-results mas-fy2022-highlights Financial year Investment gains Negative FX translation Reported net result 2021/22 S$4.0bn S$8.7bn −S$7.4bn 2024/25 S$31.4bn S$3.4bn +S$19.7bn 2025/26 update S$39.8bn S$16.4bn +S$20.0bn Published headline precision. Other costs and contributions affect the net result; these three columns alone are not a complete reconciliation. Historical uploaded evidence plus verified newer update

entries.title: Why MAS, GIC and Temasek need different scorecards
entries.text: gic-temasek Why MAS, GIC and Temasek need different scorecards Singapore They have different jobs, portfolios and measurement systems; their headline results are not a league table. MAS is a central bank and needs liquid foreign reserves for monetary policy and financial stability. GIC manages government assets for long-term global purchasing power. Temasek is an investment company that owns its portfolio assets and reports shareholder returns. Their objectives, funding arrangements and investment flexibility differ. GIC’s uploaded FY2024/25 report explains its rolling twenty-year horizon. The separately verified FY2025/26 release reports 5.6% annualised nominal USD return and 3.4% annualised real return for the twenty years ended 31 March 2026. These are compounded annualised results over twenty years, not returns earned in just FY2025/26. A rolling figure can change because an old year drops out as well as because a new year enters. The historical GIC asset mix on page 14 is useful for explaining diversification. It is not a prescription for a client. GIC’s funding horizon and ability to hold private investments are different from a household’s. Its 2026 release also announces a Strategic Portfolio framework, so the older Reference Portfolio description should not be presented as the unqualified current framework. Temasek’s uploaded 2025 highlights reported S$434 billion net portfolio value, with a further S$35 billion uplift if the remaining unlisted investments were marked to market. The same-date comparable value was S$469 billion. The 2026 release reports S$518 billion after the full transition to mark-to-market reporting. The comparable increase is S$49 billion, not S$84 billion. Keep the bridge in sequence: S$434 billion plus S$35 billion equals S$469 billion at 31 March 2025; S$469 billion plus S$49 billion equals S$518 billion at 31 March 2026. The first step changes valuation basis at the same date. The second is the change between dates. Net portfolio value movements are not automatically identical to an investment return because capital flows and shareholder distributions can matter. Temasek’s 2026 one-year TSR was 10.5% in SGD, 12.9% at constant currency and 14.8% in USD. The arithmetic constant-currency gap is 2.4 percentage points. It reflects foreign-currency exposures collectively, not a disclosed USD-only loss. Headquarters, underlying business geography and currency exposure are also different classifications. Judge a hospital, an insurer and an investment fund against their own jobs. Comparing one headline number without its mandate and measurement would miss the purpose. Do not infer full government reserves, an undisclosed GIC asset base, or each entity’s NIRC allocation from these reports. Do not treat a valuation-method change as an investment gain. Compare like periods, like currencies and like valuation methods. Use institutions to learn process and discipline, then adapt to the client’s actual liabilities and liquidity needs. gic-2025 gic-2026 temasek-2025 temasek-2026 mas-2025-accounts nirc gic-fy2025-horizon gic-fy2025-allocation temasek-fy2025-overview Historical framework with current source corrections

entries.title: Why Temasek USD and SGD bonds have different prices
entries.text: temasek-bonds Why Temasek USD and SGD bonds have different prices Bonds The payment currency, coupon and discount curve can create very different prices even with the same guarantor. The issuer’s official register confirms the four bonds below. They are issued by Temasek Financial (I) Limited and guaranteed by Temasek Holdings (Private) Limited. Temasek explicitly states that its bonds are not guaranteed by the Singapore Government. The guarantee concerns contractual payments, not a stable market price or ready resale liquidity. A USD cash flow is valued against the USD interest-rate environment and relevant issuer spread. An SGD cash flow is valued against the SGD environment. A low fixed coupon becomes less competitive when the market requires a higher yield, so the price may fall well below face value. A higher-coupon bond can trade above face value and still offer a lower yield than its coupon. The supplied bilingual report uses two snapshot dates: 14 August 2026 for the 2039 examples, and 7 August 2026 for the 2070/2071 examples. These can illustrate the mechanism but must not appear as live dealing levels. The 2039 ask prices of 118.040 in SGD and 104.092 in USD are above par, not below par. Their location below an earlier chart high is a different claim. The report’s displayed yield-gap calculations are arithmetically consistent: 2.588% − 2.313% = 0.275 percentage point = 27.5 basis points, and 4.950% − 4.890% = 0.060 percentage point = 6 basis points. These are illustrative comparisons with particular government bonds. Maturity and cash-flow mismatches mean they are not precise option-adjusted or interpolated credit spreads. Pair each price with its own quote side. In the 2070 example, 5.475% is the bid yield paired with the 50.664 bid price, not the 51.076 ask price. The 2071 example likewise shows a 2.975% bid yield. An investor buying at an ask price needs the corresponding ask yield; this cannot be inferred by relabelling the bid yield. Compare total settlement cost and expected cash flows rather than the clean price alone. Clean price excludes accrued interest; the settlement amount normally includes it. Accrued interest paid to the seller should be reconciled with the next coupon in a dated cash-flow calculation. It should not be counted twice or mistaken for a permanent change to the coupon rate. If the starting clean price is already an executable ask, do not add the bid-ask spread again; add accrued interest and only separately charged fees or costs. A financed holding has additional moving parts: borrowing rates, loan currency, recognition ratios, collateral requirements and refinancing. These must use the actual facility terms. No advance ratio or margin-call threshold can be established from these public reports alone. The same company can issue two long-term payment promises in different currencies. Their values depend on what investors require for each currency and payment schedule. A low price alone is not proof of a bargain. High credit quality does not remove duration, FX, liquidity or leverage risks, and the Singapore Government does not guarantee these bonds. Obtain current executable bid/ask prices, settlement dates and terms. Compare yield, duration, spread, spending-currency exposure and ability to hold through volatility. temasek-bonds temasek-guarantee sgs treasury Bond currency and maturity Coupon Regulation S / local ISIN USD · 23 November 2039 5.3750% US87973RAB69 SGD · 7 December 2039 4.2000% SG7U77951360 USD · 6 October 2070 2.5000% US87973RAW07 SGD · 17 August 2071 2.8000% SGXF69044257 Official issue terms, checked 31 October 2026. These are distinct bonds; do not merge a USD issue with the SGD issue sharing a similar maturity year. Verified issue terms; historical price examples only

entries.title: When a statement value is not cash you can withdraw
entries.text: alternatives-liquidity When a statement value is not cash you can withdraw Alternatives Private investments may earn returns while still limiting when, and at what price, you can recover your money. Alternatives is a broad label. Private equity owns companies; private credit lends to borrowers; real estate owns property; infrastructure owns or operates physical assets; hedge funds use varied trading strategies. Their risks are not interchangeable. The useful starting point is the economic source of return and the conditions for turning it back into cash. Private assets are often valued less frequently than exchange-traded securities. A smoother reported line may reflect the valuation process as well as the economics. It does not prove the asset would hold its value if sold immediately. Historical comparisons can also mix private-fund internal rates of return with public-market annual returns, making simple rankings misleading. JPMorgan’s page 58 shows a 4Q 2025 private-equity capital-call rate of 31% of beginning dry powder and a distribution rate of 14% of beginning NAV. These are preliminary rolling twelve-month rates with different denominators. Subtracting 14% from 31% would not calculate a valid net funding gap. A capital call asks an investor to deliver money already committed. A distribution returns cash. A fund can call capital before much cash comes back. An investor’s liquidity plan therefore needs to allow for commitment schedules and delays in exits, rather than assuming a stated annual return is spendable cash. Page 59 shows 2Q 2026 LP-led secondary pricing at 91% of NAV for buyout, 89% for credit, 79% for venture capital and 68% for real estate. These are market aggregates, not firm offers for a particular fund. A discount may reflect illiquidity, uncertainty or an out-of-date NAV; it is not automatically a bargain. Institutional portfolios can offer useful lessons about diversification and manager selection. Copying their allocation without matching their ability to meet future cash needs can create a very different risk. Liquidity is a portfolio property: even attractive long-term holdings can be unsuitable for money needed on a fixed near-term date. Owning a valuable apartment is different from having the sale proceeds in your bank account today. Timing and selling price both matter. Reported volatility, NAV, IRR, cash distributions and executable exit prices are different measures. Do not rank private products using a single yield or past-return figure. Before allocating, map capital commitments, redemption windows, gates, notice periods, valuation methods, fees and the cash reserve needed outside the investment. jpm-alternatives gic-2025 jpm-gta-p58 jpm-gta-p59 Lagged private-market observations with methodology

entries.title: Is all reported interest paid in cash
entries.text: private-credit Is all reported interest paid in cash Alternatives Some interest can be added to debt rather than received in cash, so reported income needs a cash-quality check. Payment in kind, or PIK, is a form of non-cash payment. In a loan context it often adds interest to the outstanding amount instead of paying it immediately. It can be a contractual feature rather than a default. It can also become more relevant when a borrower is conserving cash. JPMorgan page 69 shows PIK at 8.0% of interest and dividend income, on average for the Fitch-rated business development company sample, in 1Q 2026. This does not mean 8.0% of all private loans defaulted. It does not mean 8.0% of a particular fund’s assets are impaired. The population and denominator are essential to understanding the statistic. The same page compares public and private default trends with differing definitions and denominators. Private-credit defaults use counts of defaulted loans relative to loans; the public series uses issuer-based measures. Distressed exchanges also change the apparent default rate. A rewrite that strips away these differences can make a precise-looking chart misleading. For income-oriented clients, ask where the distribution comes from: cash interest, asset sales, borrowing, accumulated income or other sources permitted by the fund structure. A stated distribution rate is not necessarily a sustainable economic return. Asset-level yield and the investor’s net return can also diverge after fees, leverage and losses. The AI connection is worth monitoring, but it should be established issuer by issuer. Private financing can support productive investment; it can also concentrate financing risk in businesses whose revenues arrive later than their interest and capital spending. Aggregate charts identify questions for due diligence, not verdicts on every private-credit fund. Being told that someone owes you more is different from receiving more cash this month. Both may have value, but they fund your spending differently. PIK is not automatically default, and a lower reported default rate is not automatically evidence of a safer market if definitions differ. Review cash interest coverage, PIK share, non-accruals, amendments, leverage, covenants, recoveries and actual cash distributions at the specific fund or borrower level. jpm-alternatives jpm-gta-p69 1Q 2026 income-quality observation; not a default rate

entries.title: Build a portfolio that can survive the journey
entries.text: portfolio-actions Build a portfolio that can survive the journey Portfolio A sound long-term idea still needs enough liquidity and manageable concentration to survive difficult periods. JPMorgan’s drawdown chart covers full calendar years from 1980 to 2025. It reports an average intra-year decline of 14.2%, while 35 of the 46 years finished with positive price returns. The 2026 bar is year to date and is outside that full-year count. These are price returns, not returns including reinvested dividends. The lesson is about the route taken, not a guarantee of recovery. A good year can contain a frightening decline. A diversified index’s historical pattern does not imply that every individual share recovers, that every downturn is short, or that leverage is safe. Forced selling can make an interim loss permanent for the investor who must exit. Diversification should address sources of risk rather than product count. Inflation or interest-rate shocks can hurt stocks and long bonds together. AI-linked equities and AI-linked private lending can share a cash-flow driver. An offshore bond and a CHF loan introduce two currency exposures, and their movements should not be assumed to offset. For a reader deciding what to do, separate money by purpose before selecting products. Near-term spending requires dependable liquidity in the spending currency. Long-term growth capital can tolerate a different path. Income assets should be assessed for cash quality, while duration positions need a clear holding horizon and loss tolerance. Use rebalancing to maintain the chosen risk profile rather than allowing winners to determine it unintentionally. Review correlated exposures across direct holdings and funds. For borrowing, use the actual facility rules and stress asset prices, loan FX and financing rates together; the reports do not supply proprietary recognition rules or client-specific margin limits. The strategy implication is conditional: preserve the capacity to stay invested when the investment case remains sound, while retaining the flexibility to change course when evidence changes. This follows from the mechanics and historical evidence; it is not a recommendation to buy a particular security or copy an institution’s portfolio. A plan should fit the uncomfortable middle of the journey, not only the outcome you hope to reach at the end. Historical averages and previous recoveries are not a minimum future return or a deadline for the next recovery. Review cash needs, underlying concentration, duration, credit compensation, currency mismatch and funding resilience together. Record what evidence would change the investment case. jpm-markets jpm-alternatives mas-macro jpm-gtm-p16 Interpretation and practical monitoring
