entries.text: Market understanding | 31 October 2026 ← Back to Market Intelligence Hub Historical educational snapshot · prepared 31 October 2026 Public text-and-source-link edition integrated 3 November 2026. Original publisher screenshots and full PDFs are not hosted here while reuse terms are unverified. Open the official source links to view the originals. Some institutional material is from 2025; source-specific periods remain labelled. Rolling PDF links may now show a different edition. This is not a live market update. MARKET UPDATE / UNDERSTANDING THE EVIDENCE Understand the market. Know what the numbers mean. A plain-English guide to Singapore, global markets, bonds, currencies and private investments — with official source links and dated explanations. REVIEWED 31 October 2026 Singapore time Dated research snapshots. Published facts, forecasts and interpretation are labelled separately. 12 supplied files reviewed 19 evidence references · source links 15 plain-English chapters Official source links throughout The central idea A good asset can still produce a disappointing result. The purchase price, currency, financing and access to cash can change the outcome. Read the economy, the market price and your own cash requirements together. Growth AI supports activity; funding capacity still matters. Bonds Repayment strength and price stability are different. Currency A USD gain can shrink after conversion into SGD. Liquidity Reported value is not always cash available today. All topics Singapore Equities Bonds Currency Alternatives Portfolio Search explanations Expand all explanations Print / save PDF 15 chapters Reading guide 01 Three questions before any market headline 02 Why strong Singapore growth can still feel uneven 03 Why MAS cares about the SGD basket 04 Who pays for the AI buildout 05 Does owning hundreds of shares spread risk evenly 06 Why a strong borrower can have a volatile bond 07 Is a high bond yield good compensation for risk 08 Why a USD gain can shrink in SGD 09 Where Singapore’s government revenue comes from 10 How MAS can have an FX drag and still make a profit 11 Why MAS, GIC and Temasek need different scorecards 12 Why Temasek USD and SGD bonds have different prices 13 When a statement value is not cash you can withdraw 14 Is all reported interest paid in cash 15 Build a portfolio that can survive the journey Corrections to the drafts Plain-English glossary Official sources Publisher disclosures 01 / Start here Explanation with dated evidence Three questions before any market headline Ask what is happening in the economy, what is already priced into investments, and what reaches your own pocket. In everyday language A useful market update explains a cause, a possible consequence and a decision to monitor. It should help the reader ask a better question. Read the explanation These reports become easier to understand once the three questions are kept separate. The economy describes activity, jobs and prices. Markets put a price today on an uncertain future. Your personal outcome also depends on the price you paid, the currency you spend, fees, financing and when you need your money back. Strong growth can coexist with a disappointing investment return if buyers already paid for even better growth. A highly rated borrower can issue a bond whose market price swings sharply. An overseas portfolio can gain in its own currency yet deliver a much smaller gain in SGD. These are different mechanisms, so a single green or red headline is usually inadequate. Use the MAS October review to understand Singapore’s current growth, inflation and policy backdrop. Use JPMorgan to explain global markets and investment mechanics. Use MAS, GIC and Temasek annual reports to understand institutional roles and measurement. The three supplied written reports are secondary analyses: their claims need the underlying official sources. The reading order in this briefing follows those links. It moves from growth and inflation to equities, rates and credit, then currency, public finances, institutions and private markets. All quoted numbers retain the source’s own displayed precision. A source-published rounded figure is not converted into a falsely exact economic measurement. What this does not prove The review date of this briefing is 31 October 2026. The charts are dated snapshots, not live prices or a claim that all figures describe the same day. What to watch or do Begin each client discussion with spending currency, time horizon, cash needs and ability to withstand a temporary loss. Monetary Authority of Singapore source ↗ · J.P. Morgan Asset Management source ↗ · J.P. Morgan Asset Management source ↗ 02 / Singapore Published observations and MAS outlook Why strong Singapore growth can still feel uneven Technology is doing much of the heavy lifting; a strong national figure does not mean every sector is thriving. In everyday language Think of a company whose best division generates most of the additional profit. The company can be growing strongly while other divisions struggle. Read the explanation The MAS October review reports Q3 2026 GDP growth of 5.4% year on year and 1.1% quarter on quarter after seasonal adjustment. These are advance estimates. The two figures answer different questions: the first compares with the same quarter a year earlier; the second compares with the immediately preceding quarter after removing recurring seasonal patterns. Technology-related industries accounted for around 75% of year-on-year growth in Q3, according to MAS. That is a share of the increase in output, not a claim that technology is 75% of Singapore’s economy. The same page identifies technology-related industries as 22.1% of nominal value added in 2025. Confusing the level of activity with its contribution to growth would substantially overstate the sector’s size. The practical picture is an uneven expansion. Electronics, machinery, related trade and information services benefit from AI investment. Other parts of the economy face different demand and cost conditions. MAS describes weakness in some consumer-facing businesses and pressure on oil-related industries even while the headline economy expands. MAS expects the technology expansion to continue into 2027 at a more measured pace. This is its baseline assessment, not a promise. A slowdown in growth means output is rising less quickly; it does not automatically mean a recession. The vulnerability is that a narrower engine leaves the economy more exposed if AI spending or its financing disappoints. Source reference · image not republished Monetary Authority of Singapore · MAS Macroeconomic Review October 2026 · PDF page 21 / printed 21. Q3 2026 advance estimates. Open issuer PDF at this page ↗ What this does not prove Do not treat strong GDP as a buy signal for every Singapore company, property or fund. Sector earnings, balance sheets and prices still differ. What to watch or do Watch whether growth broadens beyond technology, whether semiconductor orders hold up, and whether jobs and household spending follow. Monetary Authority of Singapore source ↗ 03 / Singapore Published data and labelled forecasts Why MAS cares about the SGD basket Singapore uses the exchange rate to help control imported inflation; USD/SGD is only one part of that policy picture. In everyday language The same stronger dollar that makes some imported goods cheaper can make an overseas investment look smaller on an SGD statement. Read the explanation MAS Core Inflation rose from 1.5% in Q2 2026 to 2.1% in July–August. The October review forecasts core inflation of 1.5–2.0% for 2026 and 1.5–2.5% for 2027. These are forecasts for annual averages, not a ceiling on every monthly reading. Core inflation excludes accommodation and private transport; it is not identical to a particular household’s cost-of-living change. Inflation describes how fast prices rise. If inflation slows, prices can still be increasing. It is the difference between climbing stairs more slowly and going back downstairs. Energy, food, transport, wages, subsidies and competition can move differently, so the components matter as much as the headline. MAS maintained the prevailing appreciation rate of the S$NEER policy band in October 2026, after tightening in April and July. S$NEER is a trade-weighted currency measure. The bilateral USD/SGD rate is the price of one currency against another. An appreciating basket can coexist with SGD weakness against a particular currency, because the other basket currencies also move. For households, a stronger SGD can soften imported costs. For an investor with unhedged overseas assets, it can reduce the value translated back into SGD. Those effects can occur together. MAS’s policy objective concerns price stability in Singapore; maximising the SGD accounting return on foreign reserves is a different objective. The review’s inflation research separates external demand, external supply and domestic forces. It estimates that external factors explain about 68% of the inflation variation captured by its model over the sample. That is a model-based historical decomposition, not a statement that 68% of each household bill is imported. The policy implications depend on the source and persistence of the shock. Source reference · image not republished Monetary Authority of Singapore · MAS Macroeconomic Review October 2026 · PDF page 10 / printed 10. FX chart through 9 October 2026. Open issuer PDF at this page ↗ Source reference · image not republished Monetary Authority of Singapore · MAS Macroeconomic Review October 2026 · PDF page 29 / printed 29. July–August 2026. Open issuer PDF at this page ↗ What this does not prove A fall in USD/SGD alone does not measure the full MAS policy stance. Neither the basket path nor the inflation forecast guarantees a particular future FX rate. What to watch or do Separate a household’s SGD cash requirements from long-term foreign assets. Read the latest policy decision alongside inflation components and actual bilateral rates. Monetary Authority of Singapore source ↗ 04 / Equities Historical observations, forecasts and risk analysis Who pays for the AI buildout Demand can be strong while the bill for future capacity rises even faster than cash generation. In everyday language A restaurant can be busy and profitable while borrowing heavily to open many new outlets. The question is whether the new outlets eventually earn enough to justify the cost. Read the explanation JPMorgan’s page 22 groups Alphabet, Amazon, Meta, Microsoft and Oracle. It shows total company capital expenditure of US$416 billion in 2025, with consensus forecasts of US$799 billion in 2026, US$1,093 billion in 2027 and US$1,200 billion in 2028. The last three are forecasts. The measure is total company capex, not a directly measured AI-only spending total. Operating cash flow is cash generated from running a business. Capital expenditure pays for long-lived assets such as equipment and buildings. On the slide, free cash flow is operating cash flow minus capex. A company can report accounting profit while free cash flow is weak because it is spending heavily on future capacity. That does not by itself prove insolvency, but it changes the funding question. MAS provides a useful second view. Page 23 compares semiconductor production conditions with a composite indicator of hyperscalers’ capacity to sustain capex. The latter considers cash-flow margins, leverage and investment intensity. Its company universe differs from JPMorgan’s and includes CoreWeave. These are analytical indices, not an observable default probability or a reproducible bank credit score. The connection is straightforward: suppliers can enjoy strong orders today while customers take on larger financing commitments. If future AI revenue justifies the spending, the expansion may endure. If monetisation disappoints, buyers may reduce capex, lenders may demand better terms and suppliers may face weaker orders. MAS describes this as a downside risk, while judging near-term backlogs and commitments supportive. For a portfolio, inspect the shared economic exposure. Technology equities, semiconductor suppliers, data-centre property, power infrastructure and private credit to the same ecosystem may all respond to one investment cycle. Different product labels do not ensure different underlying risks. Source reference · image not republished J.P. Morgan Asset Management · J.P. Morgan Guide to the Markets U.S. 4Q 2026 · PDF page 22 / printed 22. 2025 actual; 2026–2028 consensus forecasts as of 30 September 2026. Open issuer PDF at this page ↗ · Rolling URL may show a later edition. Source reference · image not republished Monetary Authority of Singapore · MAS Macroeconomic Review October 2026 · PDF page 23 / printed 23. Chart through Q2 2026; review 13 October 2026. Open issuer PDF at this page ↗ What this does not prove Large capex is neither proof of a bubble nor proof of an attractive investment. Aggregate cash-flow charts cannot establish whether an individual borrower can service its debts. What to watch or do Track cash generation against capex, debt and lease commitments, refinancing needs, customer contracts and actual monetisation. Keep each issuer’s analysis separate. J.P. Morgan Asset Management source ↗ · Monetary Authority of Singapore source ↗ 05 / Equities 30 September 2026 snapshot Does owning hundreds of shares spread risk evenly An index can own many names while a small group still drives much of its value. In everyday language A supermarket basket with hundreds of items can still be dominated by a few expensive purchases. The number of items does not determine where most of the money went. Read the explanation At 30 September 2026, JPMorgan shows the ten largest S&P 500 constituents at 40.6% of market capitalisation and 36.1% of trailing earnings. A market-cap-weighted index puts more money into larger companies. Counting the number of holdings therefore does not tell you how evenly the risk is spread. The earnings share also matters. The largest companies contribute substantial profits as well as substantial market value. Concentration alone does not prove prices are irrational. It tells you which companies and business drivers can most influence results, and where earnings disappointment could be consequential. JPMorgan’s valuation page reports a forward P/E of 19.0 times against its 30-year average of 17.2 times. Forward P/E is price divided by forecast earnings. A higher ratio means paying more for each unit of expected profit. If the earnings forecast changes, the valuation can change even without a move in the share price. CAPE, also shown in the guide, uses a long historical average of inflation-adjusted earnings. It is a different measurement, so its number should not be compared directly with forward P/E as if one were an alternative price quote. Valuation measures help frame expectations; they do not provide a date for a market correction. For a Singapore investor, add a currency lens. A U.S. index chart generally describes the U.S. market in USD. The return in SGD depends on the exchange rate and any hedging. Owning an S&P 500 fund, a technology fund and several megacap shares may add overlapping exposure rather than meaningful new diversification. Source reference · image not republished J.P. Morgan Asset Management · J.P. Morgan Guide to the Markets U.S. 4Q 2026 · PDF page 8 / printed 8. 30 September 2026. Open issuer PDF at this page ↗ · Rolling URL may show a later edition. Source reference · image not republished J.P. Morgan Asset Management · J.P. Morgan Guide to the Markets U.S. 4Q 2026 · PDF page 5 / printed 5. 30 September 2026. Open issuer PDF at this page ↗ · Rolling URL may show a later edition. What this does not prove A historical average is not a fair-value guarantee. Concentration can persist, and expensive markets can keep rising. What to watch or do Review the largest underlying holdings across all funds and direct shares. Compare business drivers, regions, currencies and valuation assumptions before adding another product. J.P. Morgan Asset Management source ↗ 06 / Bonds Publisher illustrative scenarios Why a strong borrower can have a volatile bond Credit quality concerns repayment; duration concerns how much the price moves when required yields change. In everyday language A reliable tenant does not make the resale price of a long rental contract stable when market rents and interest rates change. Treasury maturity Yield falls 1 percentage point No yield change Yield rises 1 percentage point 2 years 6.8% 4.9% 3.0% 10 years 13.1% 5.3% −2.5% 30 years 20.3% 5.6% −9.0% Exact displayed scenario values from JPMorgan page 34. Parallel curve shift; the slide does not explicitly identify the scenario horizon. These are source illustrations, not an investor-specific simulation. Read the explanation A fixed-rate bond promises a stream of payments. If comparable new bonds offer a higher yield, buyers usually pay less for the old payment stream. If required yields fall, the old stream becomes more attractive. The issuer can remain financially sound throughout this repricing. Maturity is the date principal is due. Duration measures sensitivity to a change in yield. A long maturity and low coupon often leave more of a bond’s value dependent on distant payments, increasing its rate sensitivity. Convexity describes the bend in the price–yield relationship; it explains why a simple straight-line estimate becomes less accurate for larger moves. JPMorgan page 34 illustrates total-return scenarios under a parallel shift in the yield curve. The printed figures below show how the range widens at longer maturities. The slide does not explicitly state the scenario horizon, so these should be described as the publisher’s illustrations, not independently verified one-year forecasts. Long yields are influenced by more than the next central-bank meeting. Inflation expectations, the compensation for holding long debt, government borrowing needs and supply can all matter. MAS’s October financial-conditions chapter describes rising long government yields even alongside resilient equity markets. Holding to maturity changes the decision if contractual payments are met and the investor can hold. It does not remove inflation, currency, funding or collateral risk. A financed investor might be forced to sell before maturity, turning an interim price fall into a realised loss. This is why duration must be assessed together with liquidity and borrowing terms. Source reference · image not republished J.P. Morgan Asset Management · J.P. Morgan Guide to the Markets U.S. 4Q 2026 · PDF page 34 / printed 34. 30 September 2026. Open issuer PDF at this page ↗ · Rolling URL may show a later edition. Source reference · image not republished Monetary Authority of Singapore · MAS Macroeconomic Review October 2026 · PDF page 9 / printed 9. Data available through 13 October 2026. Open issuer PDF at this page ↗ What this does not prove These publisher illustrations are not prices or P&L forecasts for a specific Temasek or Treasury holding. They exclude the investor’s own FX, fees, financing and margin arrangements. What to watch or do Compare duration and maturity separately. Stress the relevant part of the curve, and check the cash and collateral available to survive the path. J.P. Morgan Asset Management source ↗ · Monetary Authority of Singapore source ↗ 07 / Bonds Dated credit-market observations Is a high bond yield good compensation for risk A bond can offer a high total yield while paying only a small extra amount for the company’s credit risk. In everyday language The base rental market can be expensive even when the extra rent for accepting a troublesome tenant is small. PLAIN ENGLISH The terms worth knowing GDP growth How much economic output changes; distinguish year-on-year from quarter-on-quarter measures. Core inflation An inflation measure excluding specified components; Singapore and U.S. definitions are not identical. S$NEER A trade-weighted measure of SGD against a basket of currencies; different from USD/SGD. Coupon Contractual bond interest expressed as a percentage of face value. Yield to maturity The discount rate that equates the bond’s price to its scheduled cash flows under the stated conventions. Yield to worst The lowest relevant contractual yield under the source’s call/maturity assumptions; it is not a worst possible loss. Duration Sensitivity of bond value to a change in yield; distinct from years to final repayment. Convexity The curvature of the relationship between bond price and yield. Credit spread Extra yield relative to a reference curve, with the exact definition depending on the measure. Basis point 0.01 percentage point. One percentage point equals 100 basis points. P/E Share price relative to earnings; forward P/E uses forecast earnings. Capex Spending on long-lived assets such as equipment, property and infrastructure. Free cash flow In the cited JPM chart, operating cash flow minus capital expenditure; check definitions elsewhere. NAV / NPV A reported net asset or portfolio value. Method, valuation date and liquidity matter. TSR Total shareholder return, reflecting shareholder outcomes under the issuer’s methodology. Real return Return after adjusting for inflation. NIRC The investment-return contribution available to Singapore’s budget under the constitutional framework. Capital call A request to deliver money previously committed to a private fund. Distribution Cash or assets returned by a fund; not necessarily identical to economic profit. PIK Payment in kind: non-cash interest or payment, often added to the amount owed. Liquidity Ability to turn an investment into usable cash at an acceptable price and time. Mark to market Valuing assets using current market-based measures; implementation varies for unlisted assets. entries.text: Alphabet (GOOGL) · Research watch ← Market Intelligence Hub Company research · dated snapshot Alphabet (GOOGL) Growth and cash generation. Watch only · Generated research · 3 November 2026 Static research snapshot. Prices and figures do not refresh automatically. This page records research, not an executed trade, confirmed holding or investment recommendation. GOOGL · Class A · USD $278.99 −$0.85 (−0.30%) on 2 Nov Prior regular-session close, 2 November 2026, 16:00 EST (3 November, 05:00 SGT). Not live. Unadjusted closing price. Price history source ↗ Q3 2026 revenue $127.577bn +25% year over year Quarter ended 30 September 2026; unaudited. Q3 Google Cloud revenue $30.709bn +103% year over year Company segment reporting. The cash-generation lens Investment exceeded operating cash inflow. Q3 operating cash flow of $42.290bn was below capital expenditure of $51.355bn. Their difference is −$9.065bn in free cash flow. Alphabet Q3 2026 cash generation, US dollars in billions Operating cash flow positive 42.290 billion; capital expenditure 51.355 billion shown as an outflow; calculated free cash flow negative 9.065 billion. Original chart derived from SEC filing. Operating cash flow +42.290 Capital expenditure −51.355 Free cash flow −9.065 Zero · bars use one common scale · USD billions Accessible chart data · Q3 2026 · USD billions Measure Amount Operating cash flow 42.290 Capital expenditure (cash outflow) 51.355 Free cash flow: OCF − capex −9.065 Original chart; capex displayed with a negative sign to show its cash-flow effect. Free cash flow is a non-GAAP measure, not net income. Alphabet SEC earnings release, 28 October 2026 ↗ What to track Growth is one part of the picture. Reported: Search & other revenue grew 12%; consolidated operating income rose 30% to $40.576bn. Research interpretation: Revenue growth alone does not establish investment returns. The next results should be checked for cash conversion as well as growth. Compare Search growth and Cloud profitability with this quarter. Track operating cash flow against capital expenditure. Review changes in diluted share count and capital-allocation disclosures. Risks to review: spending may precede cash returns; competitive pressure and legal or regulatory developments can alter the outlook. These are monitoring questions, not forecasts.
